prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Why hast thou nothing in thy face? Thou idol of the human race, Thou tyrant of the human heart, The flower of lovely youth that art; Yea, and that standest in thy youth An image of eternal Truth, With thy exuberant flesh so fair, That only Pheidias might compare, Ere from his chaste marmoreal form Time had decayed the colours warm; Like to his gods in thy proud dress, Thy starry sheen of nakedness. Surely thy body is thy mind, For in thy face is nought to find, Only thy soft unchristen’d smile, That shadows neither love nor guile, But shameless will and power immense, In secret sensuous innocence. O king of joy, what is thy thought? I dream thou knowest it is nought, And wouldst in darkness come, but thou Makest the light where’er thou go. Ah yet no victim of thy grace, None who e’er long’d for thy embrace, Hath cared to look upon thy face.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Why, Thou, The

outputs.L1:
Why hast thou nothing in thy face,  
Thou idol of the human race,  
Thou tyrant of the human heart,  
Thou flower of lovely youth that art?  

Yea, thou who standest in thy youth  
An image of eternal Truth,  
With thy exuberant flesh so fair  
That only Pheidias might compare,  
Ere Time had dimmed, from marble chaste,  
The living warmth his colours graced;  

Like to his gods in proud undress,  
Thy starry sheen of nakedness.  
Surely thy body is thy mind,  
For in thy face is nought to find  
But thy soft, unchristened smile,  
That shadows neither love nor guile,  
But shameless will and power immense,  
In secret, sensuous innocence.  

O king of joy, what is thy thought?  
I dream thou knowest it is nought,  
And wouldst in darkness come; but thou  
Makest the light where’er thou go.  

Ah, yet no victim of thy grace,  
None who has longed for thy embrace,  
Has cared to look upon thy face.
outputs.L2:
Why is your face so empty of expression?  
You, adored figure of humankind,  
you ruler over human desire,  
you perfect blossom of beautiful youth.  

You stand there in that youthfulness  
as though you were a visible form of everlasting Truth,  
your abundant body so fair  
that only Pheidias could have rivaled it,  
before time faded the warm colors  
from his pure marble creations.  

In your splendid bearing you resemble his gods,  
clothed in the glittering radiance of your nakedness.  
Surely your body itself is your mind,  
for your face reveals nothing at all—  
nothing except that gentle, unbaptized smile,  
which suggests neither love nor deceit,  
but only fearless will and vast power,  
hidden within a sensual innocence.  

O sovereign of delight, what do you think?  
I imagine you know that your thought is nothing.  
You might wish to arrive in darkness,  
yet wherever you move, you create light.  

And still, no one conquered by your beauty,  
no one who has ever desired your embrace,  
has troubled to study your face.
outputs.L3:
The speaker addresses a beautiful, youthful figure whose appearance is so striking that it seems almost beyond ordinary human description. His physical perfection overwhelms the observer, yet his face remains strangely empty or unreadable. Although he possesses extraordinary beauty, there is no clear sign of inner feeling, thought, or moral depth in his expression. His face attracts attention, but it does not reveal a recognizable soul.

This figure is presented as both an idol of humanity and a tyrant of the human heart. He is worshipped because of his beauty, admired as though he were an object of devotion, yet he also exerts a kind of domination over those who look upon him. His presence inspires desire, submission, and fascination. The power he holds is not intellectual or moral, but sensual: he rules through the force of physical attraction.

The poem compares his body to the ideal forms of classical divine sculpture. This comparison suggests that his beauty is not merely personal or individual, but symbolic and almost eternal. Like a statue of a god, his body appears perfectly shaped, harmonious, and removed from ordinary weakness or imperfection. He seems less like a living person with an inner life than like an embodiment of ideal beauty itself.

At the same time, the poem emphasizes that this beauty does not communicate any clear moral or emotional meaning. His perfection is not associated with wisdom, kindness, sadness, or spiritual depth. Instead, it is marked by sensual power and a kind of innocent shamelessness. He appears unaware of the effect he has on others, or perhaps unconcerned by it. His beauty is pure surface, dazzling and commanding, but ultimately unreadable.

In the end, the speaker suggests that those who are captivated by this youthful figure do not truly seek to understand him. They are less interested in interpreting his face or discovering his inner thoughts than in experiencing the physical grace he offers. What they desire most is his embrace. His body, not his mind or soul, becomes the center of attraction, and the poem closes with the idea that beauty can command devotion even when it reveals nothing beyond itself.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents an unsettling meditation on beauty by addressing an idealized youthful figure whose outward perfection seems to conceal, rather than reveal, an inner self. From the beginning, the speaker treats the figure almost as an object of worship, using apostrophe to speak directly to him as though he were present, sacred, and capable of answering. Yet this direct address also emphasizes the silence of the beautiful figure. He is looked at, praised, and questioned, but he does not truly respond. His face becomes a surface onto which the speaker projects wonder, desire, and anxiety.

Classical imagery strengthens this sense of distance and idealization. The youth is not described merely as an ordinary human being but is associated with statues, gods, and the perfected bodies of ancient art. Such references elevate him beyond everyday experience, making him appear timeless and almost divine. At the same time, they make him seem cold and inaccessible. Like a marble statue, he possesses flawless form, but that very perfection suggests a lack of warmth, inwardness, or moral depth. The classical ideal of beauty becomes both alluring and troubling.

A central tension in the poem lies in the contrast between bodily beauty and inner meaning. The speaker searches the figure’s face for signs of thought, feeling, or spiritual significance, but finds instead a kind of emptiness. The youth’s beauty is undeniable, but it does not clearly express wisdom, virtue, compassion, or self-knowledge. His features are radiant, but they do not explain themselves. This creates the poem’s unsettling effect: the more perfect the body appears, the more mysterious and vacant the inner life seems to become.

The poem therefore questions the traditional belief that physical beauty naturally reflects moral or spiritual beauty. The youthful figure possesses an almost supernatural attractiveness, yet his power does not come from intelligence, ethical feeling, or emotional expression. It comes from presence alone. He captivates simply by existing as a sensuous image: bright, graceful, and physically complete. The speaker is drawn to him not because he communicates a profound truth, but because his beauty overwhelms thought.

By the end, the poem suggests that beauty is irresistible precisely because it does not have to justify itself. The figure’s face may be empty of clear meaning, but that emptiness does not weaken its effect. Instead, it makes the beauty more ambiguous and more powerful. The youth becomes a symbol of aesthetic fascination: radiant, silent, and spiritually uncertain. His beauty promises transcendence, yet it may contain no moral or intellectual depth at all. In this way, the poem portrays beauty as both enchanting and disturbing, a force that can inspire worship while leaving the soul unsatisfied.
outputs.L5:
**Why Thou, The**

Why do we ask questions when silence sometimes feels easier? Why do we search for meaning in simple words, in old phrases, in the spaces between one thought and the next?

“Thou” is an ancient word, once used to speak directly and personally to another. It carries a sense of closeness, reverence, and depth. When we hear it today, it often feels poetic or sacred, as if the speaker is reaching across time.

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in English, yet it gives shape to the world. It points to something specific: the sky, the earth, the truth, the moment. Without it, language feels less certain.

Together, these words create a strange but thoughtful path: **Why** asks the question, **Thou** addresses the soul, and **The** defines what is before us. They remind us that language is not only a tool for speaking, but also a way of wondering, connecting, and understanding.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Victorian-style lyric poem addressing Eros as a beautiful but empty-faced idol of youth and desire, using archaic diction like “thou” and “thy.”
counterfactuals.output:
O Eros, fair and hollow-eyed,  
Thou idol wrought of rose and snow,  
Before thy shrine our dreams abide,  
And pale with incense, come and go.  

Thy lips are sweet, yet speak no word;  
Thy brow is bright, yet void of thought;  
The trembling heart, like some caged bird,  
Beats on the bars thy beauty wrought.  

O lovely mask, O golden lie,  
With garlands bound about thy feet,  
How many souls have passed thee by,  
And found thy silence still more sweet!  

Thou hast no pity in thine eyes,  
No tear within thy marble breast;  
Yet all youth’s longing round thee sighs,  
And calls thy coldness perfect rest.  

We crown thee with the wasted hours,  
We bathe thee in our blush and pain;  
We bring thee all our April flowers,  
And ask thee only smiles again.  

But thou art empty as the air,  
A god without a ghost within;  
The heaven of thy face is fair,  
Yet blank beneath its carven skin.  

Still, still we kneel—poor fools of fire—  
To thy mute grace and cruel art;  
For thou art Youth, and thou Desire,  
The face we dream, the vacant heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a formal rhymed poem in the manner of Robert Bridges about the god of love, emphasizing beauty, sensual innocence, and the absence of thought in his face.
counterfactuals.output:
**Love’s Image**

Behold the boy, with sunlight in his hair,  
And roses breathing from his careless mouth;  
His limbs are moulded of the morning air,  
His cheek is warm with odours of the South.  

No shadow of a thought upon his brow  
Hath laid the burden of our mortal race;  
He smiles, and all the world is youthful now,  
So sweet the empty wonder of his face.  

His eyes, unvisited by grief or guile,  
Are deep as waters where the lilies sleep;  
They ask not whither, wherefore, nor the while  
What vows men make, what wounds they take and keep.  

About his throat the tender light is drawn,  
As round a flower the trembling dew is set;  
He seems not born of earth, nor yet of dawn,  
But of delight that cannot know regret.  

O innocent desire, O lovely flame,  
Too fair for wisdom and too bright for blame,  
Go, touch the heart; yet leave the spirit whole,  
A rose upon the senses, not the soul.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a late-19th-century English poem that begins “Why hast thou nothing in thy face?” and continues as an apostrophe to a youthful classical statue.
counterfactuals.output:
Why hast thou nothing in thy face?  
No grief, no triumph, no desire,  
No shadow of the mortal race,  
No glimmer of its wasting fire?  
O youth of marble, coldly fair,  
With laurelled brows and sightless eyes,  
What god forgot thee standing there  
Beneath these dim museum skies?

Thy lips are hushed, yet seem to keep  
Some music from a Delphic morn;  
Thy lids, that never wake nor sleep,  
Look on, and neither bless nor scorn.  
The centuries about thee fall  
Like leaves in autumn’s ashen rain;  
Thou heedest not the funeral pall,  
The bridal torch, the crown, the chain.

O sculptured boy, whose naked grace  
Outshames our fever and our clay,  
What meadow, lost to time and place,  
First taught thy limbs the light of day?  
Did sun-bright Hellas see thee run  
By olive-slope or temple-stair,  
Ere art, more deathless than the sun,  
Made stillness of thy golden air?

We come with hearts by longing worn,  
With hands that tremble, eyes that plead;  
We bear the burden of being born,  
The ache of thought, the wound of need.  
But thou, exempt from loss and gain,  
From love’s delight and love’s unrest,  
Hast never clasped a hand in pain,  
Nor felt a sob disturb thy breast.

And yet, because thou canst not weep,  
Our tears are drawn to thee the more;  
Because thy silence is so deep,  
We cast our cries upon thy shore.  
O fair impossibility,  
O dream in Parian bondage bound,  
Thou art what man hath yearned to be,  
And what he never yet hath found.

Still stand, while empires fade and flee,  
While new gods rise and old gods cease;  
Keep thy unanswering mystery,  
Thy dreadful innocence of peace.  
For in thy blank immortal face  
Our restless souls their mirror see—  
The hunger time can not efface,  
The beauty that refuses me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic monologue to a naked Greek god or statue, comparing him to Pheidias’ marble figures and exploring the tyranny of physical beauty over the human heart.
counterfactuals.output:
O radiant tyrant of the still air,  
you stand before me bare as dawn—  
not unclothed, but completed,  
as if the last veil were imperfection  
and the body, once uncovered,  
became a law.

Were you cut from the dream of Pheidias,  
from that white thunder sleeping in marble?  
Did some reverent hand release your shoulder  
from the prison of the stone,  
your thigh from its silence,  
your mouth from the cold discipline of gods?  
You are not flesh, and yet I tremble;  
you are not command, and yet I obey.

How cruelly beauty rules the heart.  
It needs no sword, no crown, no temple incense.  
It conquers by appearing.  
One curve of the hip, one calm immortal brow,  
and the soul forgets its arguments,  
throws down its little banners of reason,  
and kneels in the dust of longing.

What justice is there in symmetry?  
What mercy in a perfect hand?  
The noble chest, the lifted throat,  
the silence of your eyes—  
all these are accusations.  
They tell us what we are not:  
brief, divided, hungry,  
made of weather and regret.  
Beside you, our mortal passions  
seem like torches in the rain.

And yet, beautiful god,  
or godlike stone,  
I know your triumph is also your captivity.  
You cannot age, and so you cannot forgive.  
You cannot desire, and so you cannot suffer  
the sweetness of being refused.  
No pulse disturbs your splendid calm;  
no tear revises your face.  
You are adored, but never touched  
by the ruin that makes love human.

Still, I confess it:  
I have felt the old surrender.  
My heart, that unruly citizen,  
has bent beneath your pale dominion.  
It has mistaken radiance for truth,  
form for fate,  
beauty for the voice of heaven.

O marble despot,  
O naked argument against peace,  
remain there—flawless, impossible—  
and let me learn, in your cold light,  
the danger of worshipping what cannot love us back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an archaic, romantic poem about Eros as an idol of the human race, whose body seems to be his mind and whose beauty overwhelms all who desire him.
counterfactuals.output:
**Hymn unto Eros**

O Eros, idol of our mortal kind,  
Before thy shrine the ages bend and burn;  
Thy flesh is fashioned of a living mind,  
And in thy glance the starry heavens turn.  

No veil betwixt thy thought and beauty lies;  
Thy body is thy spirit made divine,  
A dream that breathes, a splendour with bright eyes,  
A godlike fire in human-shaped design.  

Who looks on thee is wounded past recall,  
And counts his ruin sweeter than his breath;  
For desire, like incense, from us all  
Ascends to thee through rapture, tears, and death.  

Thy mouth is wisdom in a crimson flower,  
Thy limbs are music visible and fair;  
Thou mov’st, and time forgetteth his old power,  
Thou smil’st, and souls are taken in thy snare.  

O tyrant fair, O sovereign of the breast,  
Whose loveliness no mortal heart may bear,  
We kneel, undone, yet deem our anguish blest,  
And crown our chains with roses and with prayer.  

For thou art Love: not gentle, not our own,  
But vast as fate, and terrible as morn;  
The race of man adores thee on thy throne,  
And dies desiring what it cannot scorn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
